info.title: VpnHood Portal API
info.summary: The API a VpnHood app uses to sign in, redeem an app-store purchase, and receive its access code.
info.description:
The Portal API is the contract between a VpnHood client app and whatever backend runs the customer's account. It is deliberately backend-neutral: it speaks of sessions, accounts, products, purchases, subscriptions and access codes, and never of the billing system behind them. Today it is implemented by the `vpnhoodiap` WHMCS addon; a different backend can implement the same document without any client change.

**Flow.** The app signs in with an identity token from Google or Apple (`POST /v1/auth/sessions`) and receives an opaque session token. It buys in the app store, then posts the store's proof (`POST /v1/billing/purchases`); the portal re-validates that proof directly with the store and provisions the subscription — one synchronous call, no polling loop. The app then refreshes `GET /v1/account`, the one snapshot that carries the delivered access code and the subscription. Store webhooks drive renewals, cancellations and refunds afterwards, so that snapshot is always the current truth.

**Trust.** Proofs and identity tokens are pointers, never evidence: every one is re-verified against the issuing store or identity provider on arrival. A purchase must carry the signed-in user's own attribution id (`obfuscatedAccountId` on Google, `appAccountToken` on Apple), so a stolen store token cannot be redeemed into another account.

servers.description: A WHMCS install running the vpnhoodiap addon. The resource path follows the script path (PHP PATH_INFO), so no rewrite rule is needed. Hosts that strip PATH_INFO accept the same routes as `?path=/account`.

host.description: The WHMCS hostname of the hub or of a white-label partner.

tags.name: auth
tags.description: Sessions: sign in with an identity provider, sign out.

tags.name: account
tags.description: The signed-in account and what it is entitled to.

get.description: Proves the portal is installed, active and able to reach its database. Answers 404 while the addon is deactivated, which is how a client detects a portal that is not configured.
The OpenAPI description of the portal as installed. Point Swagger UI or a client generator straight at it.

post.description:
Exchanges an identity provider's id token for a portal session token.

The id token is verified against the provider's published keys, and its audience must be one of the OAuth client ids registered for this app. The provider must state that the email is verified — the portal matches accounts by email, so an unproven mailbox is refused outright.

If a customer account with that email already exists, the session is linked to it; a new address stays unlinked until its first purchase creates the account. Nothing here waits on a second, portal-side confirmation of the address: the provider already proved it. Where a purchase attaches to a customer account that existed beforehand, the portal's own web area stays closed for that account until it confirms the address — a purely portal-side concern that this API neither reports nor gates on.

201.description: Signed in; the session token is in the body. After a challenge completion that spent the backup code, `newBackupCode` carries the replacement — shown once, never again.

200.description: Password form only: the password is right but the account uses a second factor — no session yet. Complete with the challenge form.

401.description: Provider form: the id token is missing, malformed, expired, or not issued to this app (`invalid_id_token`). Password form: `invalid_credentials` — deliberately ONE answer for an unknown email, a wrong password and a never-set password, so the endpoint cannot be used to scan which emails exist; setting or recovering the password on the account website is the way in. Challenge form: `invalid_code` while attempts remain, `invalid_challenge` when the token is expired or spent (start over from the password).

403.description: The package name is not a registered app (`unknown_app`); the provider has not verified the email (`provider_email_unverified`); the password form's login has no account here and owns no client (`no_account` — the password grant never creates an account), or several app accounts sit on its clients (`account_ambiguous` — support merges them).

429.description: Per-IP rate limit (`rate_limited`), or the per-address cooldown after repeated password failures (`too_many_attempts`): the address waits out the configured minutes — 10 by default — and works again by itself. It fires for nonexistent addresses exactly as for real ones.

delete.description: Revokes the presented session token server-side. Idempotent: an unknown or already revoked token also answers 204, so a client can always complete a local sign-out.

get.summary: The signed-in account — the complete snapshot
get.description:
The account holds exactly one serving access code, and ONE function chooses it — the app never sees a list. The choice is RECOMPUTED ON EVERY READ and is deterministic: the store subscription for this device's own store, then a portal code being paid for right now, then the IMPORTED code (typing a code means "use this one", so it wins over anything nobody is being billed for and never over anything that is), then the other portal codes, then nothing. Within a group, a code whose clock has started comes before one that has not, then oldest purchase first. Nothing is stored as *the* selection, so no dead choice ever has to be repaired.

Every code is either **eligible** or **rejected**, and only an access-server refusal sets it. `expirationTime` is advisory display, never an entitlement decision — a clock that could retire a code could equally start an unused one early. A rejection never skips what is being paid for right now.

When the account is subscribed in more than one store, THIS DEVICE'S OWN STORE WINS: the session remembers the store the device signed in with, and a serving subscription from that store outranks any other; the newest across all stores is the fallback. Only the store that sold a subscription can manage it, so answering with a foreign one would hide the device's own subscription and leave it unmanageable.

200.description: One object: identity, THE one access code serving the account, and the store subscription behind it. One call renders the whole account page.

delete.description: Permanent account deletion. Erases sessions on every device, sign-in identities and the account row; anonymizes and closes the customer record behind the retained invoices. Nothing blocks it: recurring web billing is cancelled at the end of its paid period, stored payment methods are dropped, and one final message carries the person's premium codes to the address before it is erased — the confirmation screen warns, the mail delivers. A store subscription is deliberately left exactly as it is: signing in again brings it back by itself, and only the person can cancel it, in their own store.

204.description: The account is deleted. The presented session token is dead.

502.description: The customer record could not be anonymized or an open invoice could not be cancelled (`deletion_failed`). Nothing partial was left behind; retry or contact support.

put.summary: Fill, replace or empty the account's one upload slot
put.description:
Stores the supplied code in the account's single upload slot, or empties it when `accessCode` is null. The backend takes any well-formed code **on trust**: validity is settled at use time by the access server, never at save time here, so there is no *not found* answer and nothing to inspect in the reply. Uploading a different code replaces what is there, and every typed code fills the slot — one the account already owns included, so typing always means *use this one*. Which code the account then *serves* is a different question — ask `GET /v1/account` — and it need not be the code just uploaded.

The code's **shape** is validated (version 1, 20 digits, checksum) and a malformed string is a `400`. Shape is not validity: a well-formed code this portal never issued is still taken on trust, because only the access server can say whether a code works.

204.description: Stored. No body: the save either worked or the call failed.

post.summary: Report that the access server refused the imported code
post.description:
One bit of news, and the whole of what the ranking needs: no reason, no expiry, no observation time, and no successful-connection counterpart. Every code an account holds is either **eligible** or **rejected**, and a device meeting an access-server refusal is the only thing that sets the second.

The code travels in the **authenticated body, never in the URL** — a path is logged, cached and proxied where a bearer credential must not appear — and it is redacted out of the audit log like every other secret. Only a fingerprint is stored.

Applied only while the report is still about the account's **current** code, compared atomically: a delayed refusal that has been overtaken by a different code changes nothing. Remove-then-re-add of the same string is the one case that slips through — identical codes are the same credential and cannot be told apart here — and the recovery is one more Retry.

A rejection applies to **every entry holding that code**: the upload slot and any service delivering the same string are skipped together. It skips, it never deletes — uploading the code again through `PUT /v1/account/access-code` clears it, which is all that *Retry* is.

The code's **shape** is validated (version 1, 20 digits, checksum) and a malformed string is a `400`. Shape is not validity: a well-formed code this portal never issued is still taken on trust, because only the access server can say whether a code works.

204.description: Recorded, or ignored because the report named an occupant that is no longer there. The device cannot act on the difference.

get.summary: Sellable store product ids for one app and store
get.description:
The portal is the source of truth for **what** may be sold; the store owns the price and the localisation. A store product that is not mapped in the portal catalog does not appear here and cannot be redeemed — an unmapped purchase parks instead of guessing at an entitlement.

No authentication: an app must render its plans page before anyone signs in, and this catalog is public by construction — the same product ids are visible in the store listing. Nothing here is account-scoped.

parameters.name: packageName
parameters.description: The app's package name (Android) or bundle id (iOS).

schema.description: The distinct product ids as they exist in the store. The catalog maps one row per plan (product + base plan), but a base plan is not something an app can act on — the store enumerates those within a product itself — so the rows arrive collapsed to their products, and nothing else is carried here.

post.description:
Turns a completed app-store purchase into a provisioned subscription — one synchronous call. The response is the state alone; the delivered code and the subscription live on `GET /v1/account`.

The portal re-fetches the purchase from the store API (the posted proof is only a pointer), checks that it was attributed to the signed-in user, maps it to a plan, provisions, and only then acknowledges the purchase with the store.

**Idempotent.** The store purchase key is the anchor; redeeming the same purchase again re-answers `provisioned` for the same order and never creates a second one. Retrying after a network failure is always safe.

**202 means not yet.** `pending` — the store has not settled the payment (deferred or slow payment methods); retry shortly.

**A paid purchase is never refused for being a second one.** Prevention happens in the app, before the store's payment sheet opens: checkout is not offered to an account that is already served. Whatever still arrives paid is provisioned — the account then holds both, each serving its own store's devices, and an administrator is alerted so it can be surfaced rather than unwound. Refusing after payment only ever worked where the store auto-refunds an unacknowledged purchase, which is not true everywhere.

**Restore after account deletion.** A purchase attributed to an account that was erased may be redeemed by a NEW signed-in account presenting the same store proof: the purchase is handed to that account and the SAME subscription re-delivered — never a new order or access code. Only when the previous owner is journalled as deleted and the new account holds no other live subscription; a purchase whose owner still exists is refused with 403 `purchase_account_mismatch` as always.

201.description: The purchase is recorded; the body is its state. `provisioned` — refresh `GET /v1/account`, the snapshot carries the delivered code and the subscription, which this response deliberately does not repeat. `pending` — the store has not settled the payment yet; retry shortly. The state is not also encoded in the status line: it is a fact about the store settling a payment, not about what this request did to a resource.

400.description: Malformed request (`bad_request`), an unknown store (`unknown_store`), or a proof the store would not confirm (`purchase_invalid`).

403.description: Unregistered app (`unknown_app`), or the purchase is attributed to a different account (`purchase_account_mismatch`).

409.description: The purchase carries no attribution the portal can resolve to an account (`purchase_unattributed`). It is recorded for an administrator; nothing was provisioned.

410.description: The purchase is no longer active at the store — expired, cancelled or refunded (`purchase_inactive`).

422.description: The store product is not mapped to a plan on this portal (`plan_not_available`). The purchase is parked and an administrator alerted; it is never guessed at.

501.description: The store is known but not implemented on this portal yet (`store_not_supported`).

502.description: Provisioning failed downstream (`provisioning_failed`). Nothing is left half-created and the purchase is not acknowledged, so it is safe to retry.

503.description: Another request is redeeming this same purchase (`purchase_in_progress`). Retry shortly.

bearerAuth.description:
The opaque session token from `POST /v1/auth/sessions`, as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. It is 64 hex characters, valid for 30 days, stored only as a hash, and revocable — deliberately not a JWT.

The same token is also accepted in an `X-Portal-Token` header, for proxies that strip `Authorization`.

portalToken.name: X-Portal-Token
portalToken.description: The session token, for proxies that strip `Authorization`.

BadRequest.description: The request is malformed or missing a required field (`bad_request`).

Unauthorized.description: No session token, or it is expired or revoked (`unauthorized`). Sign in again.

UnknownApp.description: The package name is not a registered app on this portal (`unknown_app`).

NotFound.description: No such resource — or the portal is not activated on this install (`not_found`).

RateLimited.description: Too many requests from this address (`rate_limited`).

api.description: The major version this portal serves — the same one that names the path segment. A breaking change ships as a new segment (/v2) served beside this one, so an app that cannot be updated keeps working.

StoreId.description: The app store a purchase or plan belongs to.

SignInRequest.description: One of three forms, told apart by their fields. The provider form signs in with an id token and creates the account for a new email. The password form checks the WHMCS client-area password and NEVER creates an account — it only signs into one that already exists; when a second factor is due it answers 200 with a challenge instead of a session. The challenge form completes that challenge with the authenticator code or the backup code.

provider.description: The identity provider that issued the id token.

idToken.description: The provider's id token (Google `id_token`, Apple `identityToken`). Verified against the provider's keys; its audience must be one of the app's registered OAuth client ids.

packageName.description: The app's package name (Android) or bundle id (iOS). Selects which registered app — and therefore which credentials and catalog — the request belongs to.

password.description: The WHMCS client-area password. An unknown email and a wrong password are deliberately ONE answer (`invalid_credentials`) — status, body and timing identical — so nothing here reveals whether an email exists. An account that never set a password (store-created) gets the same answer; recovery on the account website is the way in.

packageName.description: The app's package name (Android) or bundle id (iOS).

challengeToken.description: The token from the password form's challenge answer. Single-use, short-lived, a small attempt budget; it can do nothing but complete its own challenge.

code.description: The authenticator code — or the account's backup code, accepted on the same step so a lost phone strands nobody. A spent backup code is rotated and the replacement returned once as `newBackupCode`.

packageName.description: The app's package name (Android) or bundle id (iOS). Must match the package the challenge was issued to.

token.description: Pass back in the challenge form as `challengeToken`.

type.description: The second-factor kind the account uses; `totp` today. The backup code is always accepted regardless of type.

accessToken.description: The session token. Send it as a bearer token on every other call.

userId.description: The account's stable, non-enumerable id, carrying no personal data. The app passes it to the store as `obfuscatedAccountId` (Google) or `appAccountToken` (Apple) so a purchase can be tied back to its buyer.

newBackupCode.description: Only after a challenge completion that spent the backup code: the replacement, shown once — nothing ever shows it again.

packageName.description: The app's package name (Android) or bundle id (iOS).

proof.description: What the store handed the app at purchase. It is a pointer, not evidence: the portal always re-fetches the purchase from the store API before acting on it.

productId.description: The purchased product id, when the client knows it.

AppStoreProof.title: App Store proof
AppStoreProof.description: Either the StoreKit 2 signed transaction (preferred) or a bare transaction id.

transactionId.description: The original transaction id, when no signed transaction is available.

Problem.description: RFC 9457 problem detail. `code` is the contract — branch on it; `detail` is prose for logs and support and may change.

ErrorCode.description: Stable machine codes. Anything unrecognised should be treated as a generic failure of its HTTP status class.

PurchaseState.description: `provisioned` — delivered; refresh `GET /v1/account` for the code. `pending` — the store has not settled the payment yet.

AccessCodeInfo.description: THE one access code serving an account, with its own clock. Reseller stock (bulk/CSV orders) never qualifies — merchant inventory, not a personal code.

accessCode.description: The code the client redeems for premium access.

expirationTime.description: The code's own clock where it can be read; null for a one-time code that has not started, or where the install cannot read it.

SetAccessCodeRequest.description: Fill, replace or empty the account's one upload slot.

accessCode.description: The code exactly as the person holds it, or null to empty the slot. Taken on trust — the access server, not the portal, decides whether it works.

ReportAccessCodeRejectedRequest.description: Which code the access server refused. Compared against the account's current code before anything changes.

accessCode.description: The code the device was serving when the access server refused it.

Subscription.description: The store subscription serving the account. The price is what the STORE charged for the current period — not a catalogue price.

expirationTime.description: When it lapses unless the store renews it.

priceAmount.description: The store's own charge for the current period.

billingPeriod.description: The recurrence as an ISO-8601 duration ("P1M", "P1Y", …).

isAutoRenew.description: Whether the store will bill the next period.

AccountSnapshot.description: The complete account: identity, THE one access code serving it (a delivered subscription credential outranks the deliberate code choice; portal billing status and expiration metadata never withdraw it, and the choice itself is never re-picked), and the subscription behind it. The app model maps this 1:1.

userId.description: The account's stable, non-enumerable id, carrying no personal data.

name.description: The billing owner's display name, when known.

accessCodeInfo.description: THE one code serving this account, whichever channel delivered it — or null.

subscription.description: Present exactly when a store subscription serves the account.
